title.en: Sound waves, echo and the Doppler effect

text.en: Shout towards a distant cliff and a moment later your own voice comes back. That is an echo. This lesson ties together sound as a vibration, its frequency ranges and the way echoes measure distance.

Sound is produced by vibrations and needs a material medium such as air, water or steel to travel; it cannot travel through a vacuum such as on the Moon.
Audible waves have frequencies between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz; infrasonic waves are below 20 Hz and ultrasonic waves are above 20 kHz.
Infrasonic waves are produced by earthquakes, ocean waves and whales; bats, dogs and dolphins can detect ultrasonic waves.
Speed of sound v = frequency times wavelength (v = f x lambda), and the speed is different in solids, liquids and gases.
Reflection of sound at a hard surface produces an echo; the reflected sound must reach the ear at least 0.1 second after the original to be heard separately.
Using an echo, distance d = v x t / 2 because the sound travels to the reflector and back.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency when the source and listener move relative to each other.

problem.en: You shout and hear the echo after 2 seconds. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, how far is the cliff?

text.en: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so total distance is 340 x 2 = 680 m.
The cliff is half of that distance: 680 / 2 = 340 m.

prompt.en: State the three frequency categories of sound and explain how an echo is formed.

requiredIdeas.en: Echo from reflection with delay at least 0.1 s

points.en: Sound needs a medium and is produced by vibrations.
Audible 20 Hz-20 kHz; infrasonic and ultrasonic outside it.
v = f lambda; echo distance d = vt/2.
Doppler effect: apparent change in frequency.
